note.explanation: A bar chart uses bars to show the values of different categories, so you can compare them quickly.
examples: If Species A has 15 plants, its bar reaches 15 on the value axis.
If Species D has 25 plants, its bar is taller than the bar for Species A.
note.checkAnswer: The value of the corresponding category.
note.simple: Each category gets a bar. The bar’s height shows that category’s value.
note.checkQuestion: What does the height of a bar show?
note.title: Reading and making a bar chart
steps: Arrange the categories and their values.
Draw and label the x-axis and y-axis.
Choose a suitable scale with equal intervals.
Draw equal-width bars, spaced evenly, to the correct values.
Label each bar with its category and value.
note.answer: A bar chart represents data using bars of different heights or lengths to compare categories.

options: The interval used on the axis
mcqs.stem: A bar chart shows the numbers of four kinds of birds. What does the height of a bird’s bar represent?
rationales: A category name is shown by the label, not by the bar’s height.
Correct: the bar’s height corresponds to the value for that category.
The number of bars shows how many categories there are, not a single bar’s height.
Axis intervals show the scale; they are not the value represented by a bar.

mcqs.stem: When making a bar chart, where are the categories usually labelled?
rationales: Correct: the x-axis is labelled with the categories.
The y-axis is labelled with the values.
The axes have different roles: categories go on the x-axis and values on the y-axis.
The x-axis shows the categories.

options: Use uneven intervals so the bars fit
Divide the y-axis into equal intervals
Put the categories on the y-axis
Make every bar a different width
mcqs.stem: How should the value axis be marked when preparing a bar chart?
rationales: Uneven intervals make comparisons misleading.
Correct: the scale should use equal intervals.
The categories are labelled on the x-axis.
Bars should have equal width and be spaced evenly.

options: Bars should touch and have different widths
Bars should be equal in width and spaced evenly
Bars should all have the same height
Bars should be drawn without labels
mcqs.stem: Which statement describes how bars should be drawn?
rationales: The bars should be spaced evenly, and their widths should be equal.
Correct: bars have equal width and are spaced evenly.
Bar heights must correspond to the different category values.
Each bar should be labelled with its category name and value.

options: The lowest value in the data
The highest value in the data
mcqs.stem: What should you consider when choosing the scale for the y-axis?
rationales: The lowest value alone does not determine a scale that covers all the data.
The number of categories is shown along the x-axis.
Correct: the scale should be based on the range of values, including the highest value.
Bar width does not determine the y-axis scale.

mcqs.stem: What information should be written along the x-axis of a bar chart?
rationales: The values are shown on the y-axis and by the heights of the bars.
Correct: the x-axis is labelled with the categories.
A chart title describes the whole chart and is not the x-axis category labels.
The order may arrange categories but does not label them.

mcqs.stem: Which action comes first when creating a bar chart using the section’s steps?
rationales: Correct: the first step is to gather the data to be represented.
Bars are drawn after organising the data, drawing and labelling axes, and choosing a scale.
Bars are labelled after they have been drawn.
The scale is chosen after gathering and organising the data and drawing the axes.

hints: Find the largest number in the fruit data.
Use equal intervals that reach at least 45; label the categories along the x-axis and fruit quantities along the y-axis.
yourTurn.question: You are given the following data set, create a bar chart to represent the number of different types of fruits sold at a market in one week:  • Apples: 30  • Bananas: 45  • Oranges: 20  • Grapes: 25  • Mangoes: 15  Ensure to label the axes and provide a title for the chart.
solution: Organize the fruit categories with their corresponding values: Apples 30, Bananas 45, Oranges 20, Grapes 25, Mangoes 15.
Label the x-axis with Apples, Bananas, Oranges, Grapes, and Mangoes.
Label the y-axis with the number of fruits sold.
The highest value is 45. Use a scale with equal intervals of 5 from 0 to 50.
Draw equal-width bars, spaced evenly, up to the values 30, 45, 20, 25, and 15 respectively.
Label each bar with its fruit name and value, and title the chart “Fruit Sales in One Week”.
yourTurn.answer: A bar chart titled “Fruit Sales in One Week”, with x-axis “Fruit Type”, y-axis “Number Sold”, and bars: Apples 30, Bananas 45, Oranges 20, Grapes 25, Mangoes 15.

example.answer: A bar chart titled “Chart: Number of Plants”, with species on the x-axis and number of plants on the y-axis; the bars show Species A 15, Species B 20, Species C 10, Species D 25, and Species E 5.

explain.title: What a bar chart shows
explain.body: A bar chart is a graphical representation of data using bars of different heights or lengths. It is used to compare the quantities of different categories. Bar charts are effective for comparing different categories and visually representing the distribution of data.

explain.title: Axes and scale
explain.body: Label the x-axis with categories and the y-axis with values. Choose a scale that covers the data range and divide the axis into equal intervals.

explain.title: Drawing and labelling bars
explain.body: Draw a bar for each category. Make the bars equal in width and space them evenly. Each bar’s height corresponds to its value, and each bar should be labelled with its category name and value.

explain.title: Using the chart to compare
explain.body: Once the bars are drawn, compare their heights to see which categories have greater or smaller values.

mistakes: Putting the categories on the y-axis instead of the x-axis.
Using unequal intervals on the value scale.
Choosing a scale that does not reach the highest value.
Drawing bars with different widths or uneven spacing.
Forgetting to label the axes or bars with their categories and values.
